query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of a ductility‐promoting element (e.g., ~5 at.% Cr) to equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW and applying a controlled heat treatment to induce nanoscale ductile precipitates will improve room‐temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while retaining the high‐temperature (≈1600 °C) mechanical strength and BCC stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW known for its excellent high-temperature load-bearing strength but poor room-temperature ductility with irradiation response only inferred computationally.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at.% Cr into the NbMoTaW composition and perform a finely tuned post-casting heat treatment designed to promote the formation of nanoscale, ductile second-phase precipitates (e.g., B2 or even an FCC-like phase) distributed within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Testing should be conducted across a wide temperature range—from room temperature (to assess ductility) up to 1600 °C (to confirm retention of high-temperature strength) and under irradiation regimes (such as helium ion implantation simulating reactor conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale ductile precipitates dispersed in the BCC matrix, which serve as defect sinks during irradiation and enable extra slip systems for enhanced plasticity at lower temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The added Cr is expected to stabilize a secondary phase in a controlled manner. This phase provides two benefits: (1) At room temperature, it offers additional deformation mechanisms that increase ductility via the activation of compatible slip systems; (2) Under irradiation, its fine dispersion allows for enhanced defect recombination and self-healing, reducing issues like helium-induced blistering and amorphization, all while the dominant BCC matrix retains its inherent high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the modified alloy should exhibit a significantly improved room-temperature ductility and reduced irradiation-induced damage (e.g., fewer/blunted helium bubbles and less amorphization), with minimal compromise to high-temperature yield performance and BCC phase stability.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature strength yet poor ductility and computationally inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to manifest at room temperature (for ductility and irradiation damage mitigation) while maintaining performance up to 1600 °C. However, the response under extreme irradiation fluences and over long-term exposures remains to be fully validated.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in ductility and irradiation tolerance, as well as the stability of the induced precipitates under combined high-temperature and irradiation conditions, are uncertain and require detailed experimental investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one of standard equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW and one modified with ~5 at.% Cr, both subjected to an identical controlled heat-treatment designed to generate nanoscale second-phase precipitates. Characterize their microstructures (using TEM/SEM) and perform room-temperature tensile tests, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) mechanical tests, and irradiation exposures (e.g., helium ion implantation at reactor-relevant energies and fluences).
measurements: Room-temperature tensile ductility (% elongation and fracture toughness)
High-temperature yield strength and microstructural phase stability (via XRD and microscopy)
Post-irradiation defect morphology and density (using TEM, helium bubble size/distribution assessments)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-alloyed specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance (e.g., similar or increased defect formation, blistering, or amorphization) compared to the baseline NbMoTaW, or if high-temperature strength or BCC phase stability is compromised, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. Materials performance is central to the satisfactory operation of current and future nuclear energy systems due to the severe irradiation environment in reactors. Searching for structural materials with excellent irradiation tolerance is crucial for developing the next generation nuclear reactors. Here, we report the irradiation responses of a novel multi-component alloy system, high entropy alloy (HEA) AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5), focusing on their precipitation behavior. It is found that the single phase system, Al0.1CoCrFeNi, exhibits a great phase stability against ion irradiation. No precipitate is observed even at the highest fluence. In contrast, numerous coherent precipitates are present in both multi-phase HEAs. Based on the irradiation-induced/enhanced precipitation theory, the excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al0.1CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion, which reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrains the formation of precipitate, respectively. In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention. In 2010, Senkov and Miracle first published RHEAs, MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW [,]. These two alloys possess body-centered cubic (BCC) structure and have excellent elevated-temperature yield strength which is around 400 MPa at 1600 °C.
